Welcome
This website contains materials for MATH 107: Introduction to Linear Algebra (3 units, GE Area 2) at Cal Poly Humboldt. Class meets face to face Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, 10:00–10:50 a.m., in FR 201.
Catalog description: Euclidean spaces, matrices and matrix arithmetic, solving systems of equations, and eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Emphasis on applications and use of computation.
This site follows three units: representing and comparing things with vectors; transforming, solving, simulating, and computing with matrices; then explaining dynamics, fitting data, and exploiting structure (eigenvectors, least squares, SVD). Daily learning objectives are on Lectures. Class outlines for later meetings will be posted before those days.

title: MATH 107: Introduction to Linear Algebra
text:
What you’ll learn
By the end of the course you should be able to:

Interpret matrices, vectors, and complex numbers, both algebraically and geometrically.
Solve systems of linear equations using row-reduction techniques by hand and with software.
Find eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix by hand for a \(2\times 2\) matrix and with software for general cases.
Understand and apply eigenvalues and eigenvectors to solve problems.
Recognize special types of matrices and their properties, such as triangular, symmetric, and positive definite matrices.
Communicate in the language of linear algebra, including linear combination, subspace, span, independence, basis, and dimension.
Write or adapt programs to implement linear algebra concepts, such as matrix arithmetic, vectors, and plotting.
Apply linear algebra to real-world problems.
Learn independently as well as collaboratively. Develop study techniques that include pre- and post-reading of class materials and be able to critically analyze and implement solutions in a team setting.

Daily objectives for each meeting are on the lectures page.

Unit I — Vectors and geometry (Lectures 01–14)
Use the Midterm 1 study guide for the full outcome list. High-priority skills for the final:

Represent data as vectors; add, scale, and form linear combinations.
Compute and interpret inner products, norms, distances, RMS, angles, and cosine similarity.
Distinguish linear vs affine models; evaluate \(a^{\mathsf{T}}x+b\) in context.
Run a small nearest-neighbor or \(k\)-means step by hand and discuss scale.
Use dependence, span, subspace, basis, dimension, and orthonormal language accurately.

Unit II — Matrices, systems, and dynamics (Lectures 18–32)
Use the Midterm 2 study guide for the full outcome list. High-priority skills for the final:

Compute \(Ax\), interpret columns, and recognize common 2D transforms.
Translate contexts into \(Ax=b\); solve small systems; read RREF (pivots, free variables, consistency).
Model \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\); compute a few steps; relate \(A^k x\) to long-run behavior.
Multiply matrices; compose transforms; compare computational orders.

title: Final exam study guide
text:
Unit III — Since Midterm 2 (Lectures 35–40)

Lecture 35 — Eigenvectors as persistent directions

Explain geometrically what makes \(v\) an eigenvector.
Verify a proposed eigenpair \((A,v,\lambda)\) by checking \(Av=\lambda v\).
Find \(\lambda\) when an eigenvector is given.
Connect eigenvectors to repeated transformations and steady directions.
Recognize that a rotation may have no real eigenvector, motivating complex numbers.



Lecture 36 — Characteristic equation, \(2\times 2\) eigenproblems, and complex numbers

Interpret \(a+bi\) algebraically and as a point/vector in the complex plane.
Perform the basic complex arithmetic needed for eigenvalue calculations.
Form and solve \(\det(A-\lambda I)=0\) for a \(2\times 2\) matrix.
Find corresponding eigenvectors (including simple complex cases at the course’s level).
Check real or complex eigenpairs by substitution.



Lecture 37 — Why did the system behave that way? (+ Lab 5 / Quiz 10 on Week 11)

Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors with software and verify \(Av\approx\lambda v\).
Use dominant eigenbehavior to explain growth, decay, or approach to a direction.
Interpret complex eigenvalues as rotation / oscillation behavior.
Observe orthogonal eigenvectors for a symmetric example when it appears.
Connect eigen-language back to earlier dynamical simulations.



Lecture 38 — When \(Ax=b\) has no exact solution

Recognize an inconsistent overdetermined system.
Formulate the least-squares objective \(\min_x \lVert Ax-b\rVert\).
Interpret the fitted vector \(\hat{b}=A\hat{x}\) as the closest attainable vector in \(C(A)\).
Interpret the residual \(r=b-A\hat{x}\) geometrically.
Distinguish an exact solution from a best approximate solution.



Lecture 39 — Least squares, data fitting, and positive definiteness (+ Lab 6)

Compute a least-squares solution with software (and check a tiny case by hand when asked).
Interpret residuals and RMS error in context.
Check that the residual is orthogonal to the columns of \(A\) (normal equations idea).
Recognize that \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) is symmetric positive semidefinite, and positive definite when \(A\) has independent columns.
Evaluate whether a fitted model is useful, not only report coefficients.



Lecture 40 — SVD, low-rank approximation, and capstone launch

Interpret \(A=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf{T}}\) conceptually (orthogonal factors + singular values).
Explain what a rank-\(k\) approximation keeps and what it discards.
Compare singular-value decay qualitatively for different data matrices.
Relate reconstruction error and storage to the choice of rank \(k\).
State a practical limitation of a low-rank model (what structure it may miss).

title: Math 107 Midterm 2 practice
text:
A. Definitions and meaning
Write a short precise answer (one or two sentences, or a formula). No long essays.
A1. What does it mean to say that \(A\) is an \(m\times n\) matrix? What size is each column of \(A\)?
A2. Give the column view formula for \(Ax\) when \(A\) has columns \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) and \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\).
A3. In one sentence: what does it mean to interpret \(A\) as a transformation from \(\mathbb{R}^n\) to \(\mathbb{R}^m\)?
A4. Name three structured matrix types from class (beyond “square”) and one practical consequence of structure for at least one of them.
A5. Translate “\(Ax=b\) has a solution” into a statement about the column space of \(A\).
A6. What is reduced row echelon form (RREF)? What are pivot and free variables?
A7. When does \(Ax=b\) have (i) no solution, (ii) a unique solution, (iii) infinitely many solutions? Answer in terms of RREF / consistency / free variables for a square or rectangular system.
A8. Write the model for a linear dynamical system used in class. What do the state \(x_t\) and matrix \(A\) represent?
A9. When is the product \(AB\) defined? What are the dimensions of \(AB\) if \(A\) is \(m\times n\) and \(B\) is \(n\times p\)?
A10. Why is matrix multiplication not generally commutative? Give a one-line reason (sizes or a counterexample idea).
A11. How does \(A^k x\) relate to the dynamical system \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\)?
A12. What does it mean for \(A\) to be invertible? How does invertibility relate to uniqueness of solutions of \(Ax=b\)?
A13. Why is solving \(Ax=b\) generally preferable to forming \(A^{-1}\) and computing \(A^{-1}b\)?
A14. Define the column space \(C(A)\) and the null space \(N(A)\).
A15. Define \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\). How does rank relate to \(\dim C(A)\) and \(\dim N(A)\) for an \(m\times n\) matrix?
A16. For a \(2\times 2\) matrix \(\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{bmatrix}\), write \(\det A\). What does \(|\det A|\) mean geometrically for the image of the unit square?
A17. True or false, with a one-line reason: “If \(\det A=0\), then \(A\) is invertible.”
A18. True or false, with a one-line reason: “If \(AB=I\), then \(BA\) must also equal \(I\) for square \(A,B\) of the same size.” (You may assume the course’s usual finite-dimensional setting.)
A19. Light review (Quiz 5): What is a basis of a subspace \(V\)? What is \(\dim V\)?
A20. For each expression, say whether the result is a scalar, an \(n\)-vector, an \(m\times n\) matrix, a set of vectors, or undefined (brief reason if undefined). Assume sizes make sense unless noted.

\(Ax\) when \(A\) is \(m\times n\) and \(x\) is an \(n\)-vector
\(A+B\) when \(A\) and \(B\) are both \(m\times n\)
\(AB\) when \(A\) is \(2\times 3\) and \(B\) is \(2\times 3\)
\(A^{\mathsf{T}}\) when \(A\) is \(m\times n\)
\(\det A\) when \(A\) is \(2\times 2\)
\(A^{-1}\) when \(A\) is singular \(2\times 2\)
\(C(A)\)
\(N(A)\)
\(\operatorname{rank}(A)\)
\(A^2\) when \(A\) is \(3\times 2\)
\(ABx\) when \(A\) is \(2\times 2\), \(B\) is \(2\times 2\), and \(x\) is a \(2\)-vector
residual \(Ax-b\) when \(Ax=b\) is consistent

title: Math 107 Midterm 2 practice
text:
B. Computational
Show your work for each calculation.

Matrices, \(Ax\), and transforms
B1. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&-1&2\\ 0&3&1\end{bmatrix},\quad
x=\begin{bmatrix}2\\ 1\\ -1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(Ax\) using the column-combination view.
B2. Same \(A\) as B1. What are the input and output dimensions of the map \(x\mapsto Ax\)?
B3. Let \[
R=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\ 1&0\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(R\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 0\end{bmatrix}\) and \(R\begin{bmatrix}0\\ 1\end{bmatrix}\). Describe the geometric effect of \(R\) on \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
B4. Let \[
S=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(S\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 0\end{bmatrix}\) and \(S\begin{bmatrix}0\\ 1\end{bmatrix}\). What kind of transform is this (scaling / reflection / shear / rotation)?
B5. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\ 0&3\end{bmatrix},\quad
B=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\ 1&0\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(A+B\), \(2A\), and \(A^{\mathsf{T}}\).
B6. Is \[
T=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 2&1\end{bmatrix}
\] symmetric? Triangular? Diagonal?


Systems, elimination, RREF
B7. Write the linear system \[
\begin{aligned}
x+2y&=5,\\
3x-y&=1
\end{aligned}
\] as \(Ax=b\). Give \(A\), \(x\), and \(b\).
B8. Solve the system in B7 by hand (elimination or substitution). How many solutions?
B9. The augmented matrix \([A\mid b]\) row-reduces to \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 2 & | & 3 \\
0 & 1 & -1 & | & 1 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & | & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\] Identify pivot variables and free variables. Write the general solution parametrically.
B10. Same RREF idea, but the last row is \([0\ 0\ 0\ |\ 4]\). How many solutions? Why?
B11. Reduce \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & | & 3 \\
2 & 4 & | & 6
\end{bmatrix}
\] to RREF. Describe the solution set of the corresponding system.
B12. For \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 2&4\end{bmatrix},\quad
b=\begin{bmatrix}3\\ 7\end{bmatrix},
\] is \(b\) in \(C(A)\)? Brief reason (no need for full RREF if you see the issue quickly).


Dynamics
B13. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0.5&0.5\\ 0.5&0.5\end{bmatrix},\quad
x_0=\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(x_1=Ax_0\) and \(x_2=Ax_1\).
B14. A two-state system has transition matrix \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0.9&0.2\\ 0.1&0.8\end{bmatrix}
\] (urban/rural fractions as in lecture). If \(x_0=(0.6,0.4)\), compute \(x_1=Ax_0\) and interpret the entries.
B15. For the system \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\) with the \(A\) from B13, express \(x_3\) in terms of \(A\) and \(x_0\) using a matrix power (do not expand the power by hand unless you want to check).


Matrix products, powers, cost
B16. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix},\quad
B=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\ 1&0\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(AB\) and \(BA\). Are they equal?
B17. With \(A\) from B16, compute \(A^2\).
B18. Dimensions: \(A\) is \(4\times 3\), \(B\) is \(3\times 2\), \(C\) is \(2\times 5\). Is \((AB)C\) defined? What size is it? Is \(A(BC)\) defined?
B19. Suppose \(a\) is a \(1000\)-vector, \(b\) is a \(1000\)-vector, and \(c\) is a \(1000\)-vector. Compare forming \((ab^{\mathsf{T}})c\) versus \(a(b^{\mathsf{T}}c)\) in words: which forms a huge intermediate matrix, and which is cheaper?
B20. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(A^2\) and \(A^3\). Guess a formula for \(A^k\).


Inverses
B21. Find the inverse of \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}
\] (if it exists) by finding a matrix \(B\) with \(AB=I\).
B22. Is \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 2&4\end{bmatrix}
\] invertible? Give two different reasons (e.g. determinant, dependent columns, or null space).
B23. Solve \[
\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\ x_2\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}3\\ 2\end{bmatrix}
\] without forming an inverse explicitly (back substitution / elimination is fine).


Rank, column space, null space
B24. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\ 2&0\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Describe \(C(A)\). Is \(b=(1,2,3)\) in \(C(A)\)? Is \(b=(1,3,0)\) in \(C(A)\)?
B25. Same \(A\) as B24. Find \(N(A)\) (solve \(Ax=0\)). Give a basis for \(N(A)\), or state that only \(0\) is in the null space.
B26. The RREF of a \(3\times 4\) matrix \(A\) is \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & 0 & 3 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\] What is \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\)? Which original columns form a basis for \(C(A)\) (pivot columns)? Find a basis for \(N(A)\).
B27. For the matrix in B26, what is \(\dim N(A)\)? Check that \(\operatorname{rank}(A)+\dim N(A)=n\).


Determinants
B28. Compute \[
\det\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\ 2&4\end{bmatrix}.
\]
B29. Compute \[
\det\begin{bmatrix}2&1&0\\ 0&-3&4\\ 0&0&5\end{bmatrix}.
\]
B30. The linear map given by \(A=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\ 0&3\end{bmatrix}\) sends the unit square to a rectangle. What is the area of that rectangle? How does this relate to \(\det A\)?
B31. Does \[
\det\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 2&4\end{bmatrix}=0
\] tell you that the columns are dependent? That \(A\) is noninvertible? That \(Ax=b\) fails for some \(b\)?

title: Math 107 Midterm 2 practice
text:
C. Applied / harder
Show reasoning. These mix ideas or need a careful choice of tool.
C1. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix},\quad
b=\begin{bmatrix}4\\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Solve \(Ax=b\).
Interpret \(A\) as a transformation of \(\mathbb{R}^2\): what does it do to the standard basis vectors?
Why does this system have a unique solution?

C2. A café stores each day as a \(3\)-vector (coffee sold, pastry sold, total items), where total \(=\) coffee \(+\) pastry.

Write a matrix \(A\) (or describe its columns) so that “feature vector” \(=Ax\) for an underlying \(2\)-vector \(x=(\text{coffee},\text{pastry})\).
Are the three feature directions dependent? How does that show up in \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\)?
Why might this hurt a method that treats the three features as independent coordinates?

C3. Dynamics and products. Let \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\) with \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\ 0&0\end{bmatrix},\quad
x_0=\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Compute \(x_1\), \(x_2\), and \(x_3\).
Compute \(A^2\). How does that explain \(x_2\)?
In one sentence: what long-run behavior do you see?

C4. Composition. A point is first reflected across the \(y\)-axis by \[
F=\begin{bmatrix}-1&0\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix},
\] then rotated \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise by \[
R=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\ 1&0\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Which product, \(RF\) or \(FR\), applies reflection first, then rotation? (Remember: \(x\mapsto Fx\) then \(x\mapsto Rx\) means \(R(Fx)=(RF)x\).)
Compute that product and apply it to \((1,0)\).

C5. Cost. You need \(y=ab^{\mathsf{T}}c\) where \(a,b,c\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(n\) is large.

What is the size of the intermediate matrix \(ab^{\mathsf{T}}\)?
What scalar do you get from \(b^{\mathsf{T}}c\) first, and how do you finish?
Which order would you choose, and why?

C6. Rank and consistency. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & 3 \\
2 & 4 & 6 \\
0 & 1 & 1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Argue that the first two columns are dependent.
Find \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\) (you may reduce or reason about independent columns).
For which of \(b=(0,0,0)\), \(b=(3,6,1)\), \(b=(1,0,0)\) is \(Ax=b\) guaranteed / possible / impossible? Brief reasons.

C7. Null space and dependence. Columns of \(A\) are dependent if and only if \(N(A)\) contains a nonzero vector. Use that fact on \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 2&4\end{bmatrix}:
\] find a nonzero \(x\) with \(Ax=0\), and write the corresponding dependence relation among the columns.
C8. Determinants and invertibility. For each matrix, compute the determinant and say whether it is invertible:

\(\begin{bmatrix}4&1\\ 0&2\end{bmatrix}\)

\(\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\ -2&2\end{bmatrix}\)

\(\begin{bmatrix}5&0&0\\ 0&-1&0\\ 0&0&3\end{bmatrix}\)

C9. Mixed “which tool?” — for each task, name the best primary tool from: \(Ax\) / column combination, geometric transform, RREF / free variables, dynamical iteration \(A^k x\), matrix product / composition, computational reordering, inverse, rank / column space / null space, determinant.



Task
Tool




“Will this \(2\times 2\) squash area to zero?”



“Is \(b\) a combination of the columns?”



“Write all solutions when there is a free variable”



“Undo a reversible transform”



“Where is the population after 10 steps?”



“Reflect, then rotate”



“Avoid building a huge outer product”



“How many independent columns?”




C10. Software interpretation. A classmate runs an RREF command and gets \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 2 & | & 0 \\
0 & 1 & -1 & | & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & | & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\] for \([A\mid b]\). They conclude “the only solution is \(x=0\).” What did they miss? Give the correct general solution.
C11. Geometry of \(\det\). Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Sketch the images of \(e_1=(1,0)\) and \(e_2=(0,1)\) under \(A\), and the parallelogram they span.
Compute \(\det A\). Does the parallelogram have area \(1\)?
Is \(A\) invertible? Relate your answer to the parallelogram not collapsing to a line.

C12. Basis refresh + column space. Let \(V=C(A)\) for \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&3\\ 0&0&0\\ 1&2&3\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Find a basis for \(V\) and \(\dim V\).
Is \((1,0,1)\) in \(V\)? Is \((1,1,1)\) in \(V\)?
Find a basis for \(N(A)\).

C13. Build a transition matrix. Two classrooms: each day, \(80\%\) of students in Room 1 stay, \(20\%\) move to Room 2; \(70\%\) in Room 2 stay, \(30\%\) move to Room 1. Let \(x_t=(r_1,r_2)\) be the counts (or fractions) in the two rooms.

Write the matrix \(A\) in \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\).
If \(x_0=(100,0)\), compute \(x_1\).
Does \(A\) preserve the total number of students? Check \(x_1\) entries sum.

Answers
Check only after a closed-book attempt. Update your definitions/formulas list for every miss.

A — Definitions (key points)
A1. \(A\) has \(m\) rows and \(n\) columns; each column is an \(m\)-vector.
A2. \(Ax=x_1 a_1+\cdots+x_n a_n\).
A3. \(A\) maps each input \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) to the output \(Ax\in\mathbb{R}^m\).
A4. e.g. identity, diagonal, triangular, symmetric, sparse, zero — sparse saves storage/ops; triangular makes determinants/back-substitution easy; etc.
A5. \(b\in C(A)\) (equivalently: \(b\) is a linear combination of the columns).
A6. RREF is a row-echelon form with pivots \(1\) and zeros above/below pivots. Pivot variables correspond to pivot columns; free variables are the non-pivot unknowns.
A7. (i) inconsistent row \([0\ \cdots\ 0\mid c]\) with \(c\neq 0\); (ii) consistent and no free variables; (iii) consistent with at least one free variable.
A8. \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\); \(x_t\) is the state, \(A\) is the transition / update matrix.
A9. Inner dimensions match (\(A\)’s columns \(=\) \(B\)’s rows); \(AB\) is \(m\times p\).
A10. Order matters: \(AB\) and \(BA\) need not both be defined, and even when both are, they need not be equal.
A11. \(x_k=A^k x_0\) (after \(k\) steps).
A12. There exists \(A^{-1}\) with \(AA^{-1}=A^{-1}A=I\). For square \(A\), invertible iff \(Ax=b\) has a unique solution for every \(b\).
A13. Forming \(A^{-1}\) is more work / less stable; solving the system directly is the standard approach.
A14. \(C(A)=\operatorname{span}\{\text{columns of }A\}\); \(N(A)=\{x:Ax=0\}\).
A15. Rank \(=\) dimension of the column space (\(=\) number of pivots). For \(m\times n\) matrix: \(\dim C(A)=\operatorname{rank}(A)\) and \(\dim N(A)=n-\operatorname{rank}(A)\).
A16. \(ad-bc\); absolute value \(=\) area scaling factor for the unit square (signed area accounts for orientation).
A17. False — \(\det A=0\) means noninvertible.
A18. True (in this course’s finite-dimensional square-matrix setting): a one-sided inverse is a two-sided inverse.
A19. Independent spanning list; dimension \(=\) number of vectors in any basis.
A20. (a) \(m\)-vector (b) \(m\times n\) matrix (c) undefined — inner dimensions \(3\neq 2\) (d) \(n\times m\) matrix (e) scalar (f) undefined — singular, no inverse (g) set of vectors (h) set of vectors (i) scalar (nonnegative integer) (j) undefined — \(A\) is not square / \(A A\) sizes fail (k) \(2\)-vector (l) \(m\)-vector that is \(0\) when consistent (here the zero vector)


B — Easy computations
B1. \(Ax=2\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 0\end{bmatrix}+1\begin{bmatrix}-1\\ 3\end{bmatrix}+(-1)\begin{bmatrix}2\\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1\\ 2\end{bmatrix}\).
B2. Input \(\mathbb{R}^3\), output \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
B3. \(R e_1=(0,1)\), \(R e_2=(-1,0)\); \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise rotation.
B4. \(S e_1=(1,0)\), \(S e_2=(2,1)\); shear (horizontal shear).
B5. \(A+B=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\ 1&3\end{bmatrix}\); \(2A=\begin{bmatrix}4&0\\ 0&6\end{bmatrix}\); \(A^{\mathsf{T}}=A\) (already symmetric diagonal).
B6. Symmetric: yes. Triangular: no. Diagonal: no.
B7. \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 3&-1\end{bmatrix}\), \(x=\begin{bmatrix}x\\ y\end{bmatrix}\), \(b=\begin{bmatrix}5\\ 1\end{bmatrix}\).
B8. Unique solution: e.g. \(x=1\), \(y=2\) (check: \(1+4=5\), \(3-2=1\)).
B9. Pivots \(x_1,x_2\); free \(x_3=t\). General: \(x=(3-2t,\ 1+t,\ t)\).
B10. No solutions — inconsistent (\(0=4\)).
B11. RREF \(\begin{bmatrix}1&2&|&3\\ 0&0&|&0\end{bmatrix}\); infinitely many: \(x_1=3-2t\), \(x_2=t\).
B12. No — second row of \(A\) is \(2\times\) first, but \(7\neq 2\cdot 3\).
B13. \(x_1=(0.5,0.5)\); \(x_2=(0.5,0.5)\).
B14. \(x_1=(0.9\cdot 0.6+0.2\cdot 0.4,\ 0.1\cdot 0.6+0.8\cdot 0.4)=(0.62,0.38)\); urban / rural fractions tomorrow.
B15. \(x_3=A^3 x_0\).
B16. \(AB=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\ 1&0\end{bmatrix}\), \(BA=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\ 1&2\end{bmatrix}\); not equal.
B17. \(A^2=\begin{bmatrix}1&4\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}\).
B18. Yes, size \(4\times 5\); yes, \(A(BC)\) also \(4\times 5\).
B19. \((ab^{\mathsf{T}})c\) builds a \(1000\times 1000\) matrix; \(a(b^{\mathsf{T}}c)\) only needs a dot product then a scale — much cheaper.
B20. \(A^2=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}\), \(A^3=\begin{bmatrix}1&3\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}\); \(A^k=\begin{bmatrix}1&k\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}\).
B21. \(B=\begin{bmatrix}1&-2\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}\) (check \(AB=I\)).
B22. Not invertible: \(\det=0\); columns dependent (\(c_2=2c_1\)); nontrivial null space, e.g. \((2,-1)\).
B23. From second row \(x_2=2\); first row \(x_1+x_2=3\) so \(x_1=1\).
B24. \(C(A)=\operatorname{span}\{(1,2,0),(0,0,1)\}=\{(x,2x,z)\}\). \((1,2,3)\): yes; \((1,3,0)\): no (middle entry must be twice the first).
B25. \(Ax=0\) forces \(x_1=0\), \(x_2=0\); \(N(A)=\{0\}\) (two pivot columns; only the trivial null vector).
B26. Rank \(2\); pivot columns 1 and 3 of the original \(A\). Free variables \(x_2=s\), \(x_4=t\). From RREF: \(x_1+2s+3t=0\), \(x_3-t=0\), so \[
x=s\begin{bmatrix}-2\\ 1\\ 0\\ 0\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}-3\\ 0\\ 1\\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Basis for \(N(A)\): those two vectors.
B27. \(\dim N(A)=2\); \(2+2=4=n\).
B28. \(12-2=10\).
B29. Product of diagonal: \(2\cdot(-3)\cdot 5=-30\).
B30. Area \(6\); equals \(|\det A|=6\).
B31. Yes; yes; yes (column space is not all of \(\mathbb{R}^2\)).


C — Harder
C1. (a) \(x_2=2\), \(x_1=2\). (b) \(e_1\mapsto e_1\), \(e_2\mapsto(1,1)\) — shear. (c) Square invertible matrix / unique RREF pivots in both columns / \(\det A=1\neq 0\).
C2. (a) e.g. \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\ 0&1\\ 1&1\end{bmatrix}\). (b) Yes — third row \(=\) sum of first two; \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=2\). (c) Redundant feature double-counts / distorts distance-based methods.
C3. (a) \(x_1=(1,0)\), \(x_2=(0,0)\), \(x_3=(0,0)\). (b) \(A^2=0\), so \(x_2=A^2 x_0=0\). (c) Dies to zero in two steps.
C4. (a) \(RF\). (b) \(RF=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\ -1&0\end{bmatrix}\); \((RF)(1,0)=(0,-1)\).
C5. (a) \(n\times n\). (b) Scalar \(b^{\mathsf{T}}c\), then multiply by \(a\). (c) \(a(b^{\mathsf{T}}c)\) — avoids the huge matrix.
C6. (a) Column 2 \(=2\times\) column 1. (b) \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=2\) (e.g. columns 1 and 3 are independent; column 2 is redundant). (c) \(b=(0,0,0)\) always solvable; \(b=(3,6,1)\) is column 3, so solvable; \(b=(1,0,0)\) not in \(C(A)\) (any combination has second entry equal to twice the first).
C7. e.g. \(x=(2,-1)\); \(2c_1-c_2=0\).
C8. (i) \(8\), invertible; (ii) \(0\), not invertible; (iii) \(-15\), invertible.
C9. Determinant; column space / \(Ax=b\); RREF / free variables; inverse; dynamical iteration \(A^k x\); matrix product / composition; computational reordering; rank / independent columns.
C10. Free variable \(x_3=t\); solution \(x=(-2t,\ t,\ t)\), not only zero.
C11. (a) Images \((1,0)\) and \((1,1)\); parallelogram is the unit-area shear of the square. (b) \(\det A=1\); area \(1\). (c) Yes invertible — parallelogram has positive area / does not collapse.
C12. (a) Basis e.g. \(\{(1,0,1)\}\); \(\dim=1\). (b) \((1,0,1)\) yes; \((1,1,1)\) no (middle entry). (c) \(x_1+2x_2+3x_3=0\); basis e.g. \(\{(-2,1,0),(-3,0,1)\}\).
C13. (a) \(A=\begin{bmatrix}0.8&0.3\\ 0.2&0.7\end{bmatrix}\) (columns: where each room’s students go — column 1 from Room 1, column 2 from Room 2). (b) \(x_1=(80,20)\). (c) Yes — total \(100\) preserved (columns sum to \(1\)).

title: Midterm 2 study guide
text:
Learning outcomes (Lectures 18–32)

Light review — Quiz 5 / basis (Lecture 14)

Explain what a basis accomplishes and what dimension means.
Identify a basis and dimension in simple examples.
Use span, independence, basis, and dimension accurately when they reappear with matrices (column space, null space, rank).



Lecture 18 — Matrices as data and structured objects

Identify matrix dimensions, rows, columns, and entries.
Represent datasets, networks, images, or systems as matrices.
Perform matrix addition, scaling, and transposition.
Recognize zero, identity, diagonal, triangular, symmetric, and sparse matrices.
Explain one practical consequence of matrix structure.



Lecture 19 — Matrix-vector multiplication

Compute \(Ax\) by hand for a small matrix.
Interpret \(Ax\) as a linear combination of the columns of \(A\).
Interpret \(A\) as an input-output transformation.
Explain how the dimensions of \(A\) determine the input and output spaces.



Lecture 20 — Transforming space (+ Lab 3)

Predict the effect of scaling, reflection, shear, and rotation matrices.
Apply matrices to many 2D or 3D points at once.
Plot and compare original and transformed objects.
Adapt a short program that implements a transformation.
Interpret a matrix as a coordinate or physical-space transformation.



Lecture 21 — Systems and \(Ax=b\)

Translate equations or contextual constraints into \(Ax=b\).
Interpret \(Ax=b\) as asking whether \(b\) belongs to the span of the columns of \(A\).
Classify systems as square, underdetermined, or overdetermined.
Anticipate circumstances producing zero, one, or many solutions.



Lecture 22 — Gaussian elimination

Perform elementary row operations.
Reduce a small augmented matrix to echelon form.
Solve a small system using back substitution.
Explain why row operations preserve the solution set.



Lecture 23 — RREF, pivots, free variables, and software

Interpret reduced row echelon form.
Identify pivot and free variables.
Describe a solution set parametrically.
Distinguish inconsistent, unique, and infinite-solution cases.
Use software to solve or row-reduce a system and verify with a residual.



Lecture 24 — Linear dynamical systems

Represent an evolving system as \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\).
Interpret the state vector and transition matrix.
Build a transition matrix from a flow description.
Compute and interpret the next few states.



Lecture 25 — Simulation and long-run behavior

Simulate many time steps computationally.
Plot state components through time.
Recognize stabilization, growth, decay, or oscillation.
Conduct a simple what-if simulation.
State limitations of a linear dynamical model.



Lecture 26 — Predict a system through time (+ Lab 4)

Implement a linear dynamical model.
Write or complete a short iterative calculation.
Validate the first steps by hand.
Compare results under altered parameters or initial states.
Record an unexplained long-run pattern for later investigation (eigenvalues come later).



Lecture 27 — Matrix multiplication

Determine whether a product is defined and give its dimensions.
Compute a small matrix product.
Interpret \(ABx\) as a sequence of transformations.
Explain why matrix multiplication is generally not commutative.



Lecture 28 — Composition and matrix powers

Combine multistage processes using a matrix product.
Connect \(A^k x\) to repeated dynamics.
Interpret selected entries of a matrix product or power.
Recognize how network and transition information accumulates through powers.



Lecture 29 — Computational cost

Compare algebraically equivalent orders of computation.
Count intermediate values that must be stored.
Measure runtime for increasing problem sizes.
Explain why forming a large intermediate matrix may be wasteful.
Choose a computational order and justify it quantitatively.



Lecture 30 — Inverses and solving

Interpret an inverse as undoing a transformation.
Determine whether a simple matrix is invertible.
Connect invertibility to uniqueness of \(Ax=b\).
Explain why solving \(Ax=b\) is generally preferable computationally to explicitly calculating \(A^{-1}\).



Lecture 31 — Rank, column space, null space

Interpret column space and null space through \(Ax=b\) and \(Ax=0\).
Determine rank from pivots or independent columns.
Find simple bases for column or null spaces.
Connect rank to consistency, independence, and dimension.
Use subspace, basis, dimension, rank, column space, and null space correctly.



Lecture 32 — Determinants, geometry, and invertibility

Compute determinants of \(2\times 2\) and simple triangular matrices.
Interpret determinant magnitude as area or volume scaling.
Connect determinant zero with lost dimension and noninvertibility.
Recognize the determinant of a triangular matrix from its diagonal.
Connect determinants to the coming characteristic equation (preview only).

title: Lecture 29 — Same mathematics, very different computational cost
text:
Warm-up
Let \(a=(1,2)\), \(b=(3,4)\), \(c=(1,-1)\) (column vectors).

Form the outer product \(ab^{\mathsf{T}}\) (a \(2\times 2\) matrix).
Compute \((ab^{\mathsf{T}})c\) and \(a(b^{\mathsf{T}}c)\). Same vector?

title: Lecture 29 — Same mathematics, very different computational cost
text:
Fill in
Associativity. For compatible sizes, \((XY)z=X(Yz)\). In particular, for \(n\)-vectors \(a,b,c\), \[
(ab^{\mathsf{T}})c = a(b^{\mathsf{T}}c).
\] Same mathematical result — different \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\).
Order 1 — form the matrix first. Compute \(M=ab^{\mathsf{T}}\) (\(n\times n\)), then \(Mc\).

Intermediate storage: about \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) numbers (the whole matrix \(M\)).
Cost idea: building \(M\) and multiplying by \(c\) scales like \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) work (order \(n^2\)).

Order 2 — scalar first. Compute \(s=b^{\mathsf{T}}c\) (one number), then \(sa\).

Intermediate storage: the scalar \(s\), plus the vectors — order \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\) numbers, not \(n^2\).
Cost idea: two inner/scale passes — order \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\) work.

Why wasteful? Forming \(ab^{\mathsf{T}}\) materializes a dense \(n\times n\) matrix you may never need as an object; then you immediately collapse it with \(c\). Capstone theme: choose an algorithm that matches the structure, not only the formula on the page.
Runtime. In software you can time both orders for growing \(n\) and justify which order to use with measured times (and storage counts).

title: Lecture 29 — Same mathematics, very different computational cost
text:
Worked in class
W1. Algebra. With \(a=(2,0,-1)\), \(b=(1,1,1)\), \(c=(1,0,1)\), compute \(s=b^{\mathsf{T}}c\) and \(a(b^{\mathsf{T}}c)\). Then form \(ab^{\mathsf{T}}\) and \((ab^{\mathsf{T}})c\). Match?
W2. Storage count. For general \(n\), how many entries does \(ab^{\mathsf{T}}\) have? How many numbers do you store for the scalar-first method beyond the three input vectors?
W3. Choose an order. You need \(y=(ab^{\mathsf{T}})c\) for \(n=5000\) once. Which order do you run, and what two quantitative reasons (storage + flops/runtime idea) support the choice?
W4 (preview). Sketch what a timing table should look like: rows \(n=200,1000,3000\); columns “form \(ab^{\mathsf{T}}\) then multiply” vs “scalar first.” What qualitative pattern do you expect?

NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \(b^{\mathsf{T}}c=2\cdot 0+1\cdot 1+3\cdot 1=4\), so \(a(b^{\mathsf{T}}c)=4a=(4,-4,0)\). The matrix route gives the same: \[
ab^{\mathsf{T}}=\begin{bmatrix}2&1&3\\-2&-1&-3\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad
(ab^{\mathsf{T}})c=(4,-4,0).
\]
Y2. Order 1 stores \(n^2=10{,}000\) entries in \(ab^{\mathsf{T}}\). Order 2 stores one scalar \(s\) as the essential intermediate (beyond the inputs).
Y3. Associativity preserves the value but not the work: different parenthesizations create different intermediates (e.g. an \(n\times n\) matrix vs a scalar), so flops and memory — and therefore runtime — can differ by orders of magnitude.

title: Lecture 31 — Rank, column space, null space, and basis connections
text:
Warm-up
Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & 3 \\
2 & 4 & 6 \\
0 & 1 & 1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Are the three columns independent? (Look carefully at columns 1 and 2.)
For which \(b\) can \(Ax=b\) have a solution — any \(b\) in \(\mathbb{R}^3\), or only some?

title: Lecture 31 — Rank, column space, null space, and basis connections
text:
Fill in
The column space \(C(A)\) is the span of the columns of \(A\). Solving \(Ax=b\) asks: is \(b\) in \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\)?
The null space \(N(A)\) is the set of solutions of \(Ax=\underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}\). It always contains \(0\); nontrivial null vectors mean dependent columns.
A subspace is a nonempty set closed under addition and scaling. Both \(C(A)\) and \(N(A)\) are subspaces.
A basis is a linearly independent spanning set. The dimension of a subspace is the number of vectors in any basis.
The rank of \(A\) is \[
\operatorname{rank}(A) = \underline{\hspace{3.6cm}}
\] (equivalently: number of pivot columns after elimination / RREF). Then \[
\dim C(A)=\operatorname{rank}(A),\qquad \dim N(A)=n-\operatorname{rank}(A)
\] for an \(m\times n\) matrix (number of free variables \(=\) nullity).
Reading RREF for bases.

Pivot columns of the original \(A\) form a basis for \(C(A)\).
Free-variable special solutions form a basis for \(N(A)\).







NoteEnrichment (not on quizzes)



Strang’s other two subspaces: the row space \(C(A^{\mathsf{T}})\) and left nullspace \(N(A^{\mathsf{T}})\). Same rank story; we do not drill them for Quiz 10 / Midterm 2.

title: Lecture 31 — Rank, column space, null space, and basis connections
text:
Worked in class
W1. Column space via \(Ax=b\). Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\2&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Describe \(C(A)\) in words. Is \(b=(1,2,3)\) in \(C(A)\)? Is \(b=(1,3,0)\)?
W2. Null space. Same \(A\). Solve \(Ax=0\). Give a basis for \(N(A)\) (it may be \(\{0\}\) only — say so).
W3. Rank from pivots. The RREF of \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & 3 \\
2 & 4 & 6 \\
0 & 1 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\] is \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 1 \\
0 & 1 & 1 \\
0 & 0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\] What is \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\)? Which columns of the original \(A\) form a basis for \(C(A)\)? Find a basis for \(N(A)\).
W4. Dictionary. Match each phrase to the right idea: consistency of \(Ax=b\); uniqueness of the solution when it exists; “how big is the column space?”

title: Lecture 31 — Rank, column space, null space, and basis connections
text:
Your turn
Y1. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 \\
-1 & -2 \\
0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\] Find \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\) and a basis for \(C(A)\). Is \(b=(2,-2,0)\) in \(C(A)\)?
Y2. For the same \(A\), find a basis for \(N(A)\). How many free variables?
Y3. True or false: if \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=n\) for an \(m\times n\) matrix with \(m\ge n\), then \(Ax=0\) has only the zero solution.
Y4. True or false: row space and left nullspace will appear on Quiz 10.






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. Columns: \(a_2=2a_1\), so \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=1\). Basis for \(C(A)\): \(\{(1,-1,0)\}\) (or any nonzero multiple). Yes — \(b=2a_1\).
Y2. \(Ax=0\) means \(x_1+2x_2=0\), so \(x=(-2t,\,t)=t(-2,1)\). Basis for \(N(A)\): \(\{(-2,1)\}\). One free variable; \(\dim N(A)=1=2-\operatorname{rank}(A)\).
Y3. True. Full column rank means no free variables, so \(N(A)=\{0\}\).
Y4. False. Enrichment only — not quiz material.

title: Lecture 32 — Determinants, geometry, and invertibility
text:
Warm-up
Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix},\qquad
B=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{bmatrix}.
\]

What does \(x\mapsto Ax\) do to the unit square? What is the area of the image?
Are the columns of \(B\) independent? Guess whether \(B\) is invertible.

title: Lecture 32 — Determinants, geometry, and invertibility
text:
Fill in
For \(A=\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}\), \[
\det A = ad-bc.
\] Geometrically, \(|\det A|\) is the \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) scaling factor of the unit square under \(x\mapsto Ax\) (signed area encodes orientation).
Triangular / diagonal. If \(T\) is upper or lower triangular (including diagonal), \[
\det T = \underline{\hspace{3.2cm}}.
\]
Invertibility. For square \(A\): \[
A\text{ invertible}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \det A \neq \underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}.
\] If \(\det A=0\), the image of the unit cube/square is \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) (lost dimension): columns are dependent, \(Ax=b\) fails for some \(b\), and \(N(A)\) is nontrivial.
Product rule (preview). \(\det(AB)=(\det A)(\det B)\). Useful later for compositions.
Coming attraction. Eigenvalues solve \(\det(A-\lambda I)=0\) — the characteristic equation. Today’s \(\det\) is the tool; Week 13 builds the theory.

title: Lecture 32 — Determinants, geometry, and invertibility
text:
Worked in class
W1. Compute.

\(\det\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix}\)
\(\det\begin{bmatrix}1&4&0\\0&-2&5\\0&0&3\end{bmatrix}\)
\(\det\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\4&2\end{bmatrix}\)

W2. Area scaling. Let \(A=\begin{bmatrix}0&-2\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\). Compute \(\det A\). Where do \(e_1\) and \(e_2\) go? What area does the unit square map to?
W3. Zero determinant. Explain, in one sentence each, why \(\det\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{bmatrix}=0\) means (i) noninvertible and (ii) the image of the unit square has area zero.
W4. Link to Monday. For invertible \(2\times 2\) \(A\), the formula for \(A^{-1}\) has \(\det A\) in the denominator. What goes wrong if \(\det A=0\)?
W5. Characteristic preview. For \(A=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix}\), expand \(\det(A-\lambda I)\) as a quadratic in \(\lambda\). (No need to “solve eigenvalues” yet — just form the polynomial.)

Your turn

Y2. Let \(A=\operatorname{diag}(2,-1)\). What is \(|\det A|\)? Interpret as area scaling of the unit square.

Y1. \(\det\begin{bmatrix}4&-1\\2&3\end{bmatrix}=12-(-2)=14\). Lower triangular: \(\det=(-1)(5)(2)=-10\).
Y2. \(|\det A|=|(2)(-1)|=2\): the unit square is mapped to a rectangle of area \(2\) (stretched by \(2\) horizontally and reflected/flipped vertically).
Y3. True. Singular means no unique solution for any \(b\): if \(b\in C(A)\) there are infinitely many solutions; otherwise none.

title: Lecture 37 — Why did the system behave that way?
text:
Warm-up
Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1.1&0.2\\0.1&0.8\end{bmatrix},\qquad
v=\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix}.

title: Lecture 37 — Why did the system behave that way?
text:
Fill in
Software eigenpairs. Octave eig(A) / Python np.linalg.eig(A) return eigenvalues and a matrix whose columns are eigenvectors.
Verify. For each reported pair \((\lambda,v)\), check \[
Av \approx \underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}
\] (componentwise; floating-point noise is expected). Never trust a bare printout without this check.
Dominant behavior. If \(|\lambda_1|>|\lambda_2|\ge\cdots\) and \(x_0\) has a component along the \(\lambda_1\)-eigenvector, then for large \(t\) \[
A^t x_0 \approx c\,\lambda_1^t\,v_1.
\] That explains Lab 4-style growth/decay/stabilization once you know the eigenpairs.
Complex eigenvalues. For a real matrix, nonreal eigenvalues come in conjugate pairs. In the real plane they produce \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) (rotation / oscillation), matching Monday’s pure-rotation example.
Normal modes (demo, not a DE course). For a symmetric mass–spring style matrix, eigenvectors are often \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) (orthogonal). Software shows the modes; we do not derive differential equations today.

title: Lecture 37 — Why did the system behave that way?

Worked in class

# Octave:  [V,D] = eig(A)     or    eig(A)

Read off \(\lambda\)’s and columns of \(V\). Verify \(A v_1=\lambda_1 v_1\) for one column.
W2. Explain a simulation. Same \(A\) as W1; \(x_0=(1,0)\). Using eigenpairs, explain in one sentence why \(x_t\) grows and which direction it approaches.
W3. Complex / oscillation. Software on \(R=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\) should report eigenvalues near \(\pm i\). Connect that to the cycling you saw in Lab 4 stretch / Lecture 35.
W4. Symmetric demo. Let \(S=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}\) (symmetric). Check that the two eigenvectors from W1 are orthogonal (\(v_1^{\mathsf{T}}v_2=0\)). Normal-mode pictures use the same idea in higher dimension.

title: Lecture 38 — When \(Ax=b\) has no exact solution
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Recognize an inconsistent overdetermined system.
Formulate the least-squares objective \(\min_x \lVert Ax-b\rVert\).
Interpret the fitted vector as the closest attainable vector.
Interpret the residual geometrically.
Distinguish an exact solution from a best approximate solution.

title: Lecture 38 — When \(Ax=b\) has no exact solution
text:
Warm-up
Consider the overdetermined system \(Ax=b\) with \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix},\qquad
b=\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\\2\end{bmatrix}.
\]

How many equations? How many unknowns? Is \(A\) tall, wide, or square?
Suppose someone guesses \(x=(1,0.5)\). Compute \(Ax\) and \(Ax-b\). Is \(x\) an exact solution?

title: Lecture 38 — When \(Ax=b\) has no exact solution
text:
Fill in
Overdetermined / inconsistent. When there are more independent equations than unknowns, \(Ax=b\) often has \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) exact solution. The right-hand side \(b\) may lie outside the column space \(C(A)\).
Least-squares idea. Instead of insisting on \(Ax=b\), choose \(\hat{x}\) to make \(A\hat{x}\) as close as possible to \(b\): \[
\hat{x}\;=\;\arg\min_x\;\lVert Ax-b\rVert.
\] The vector \(\hat{b}=A\hat{x}\) is the \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) attainable right-hand side in \(C(A)\).
Residual. The residual is \[
r = b - A\hat{x}
\] (some texts write \(A\hat{x}-b\); same length \(\|r\|\)). Geometrically, \(r\) is the leftover after projecting \(b\) onto \(C(A)\) — it is orthogonal to every column of \(A\) at a minimizer (Wednesday).
Exact vs approximate.







Situation
Meaning




Exact solution
\(Ax=b\) for some \(x\) \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(b\in\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\)


Least-squares solution
minimizes \(\|Ax-b\|\); residual may be \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\)



If an exact solution exists, it is also a least-squares solution (residual zero).

title: Lecture 38 — When \(Ax=b\) has no exact solution
text:
Worked in class
W1. Inconsistent check. For the warm-up \(A\) and \(b\), argue that no \(x=(x_1,x_2)\) can satisfy all three equations simultaneously. (Hint: equations 1–2 force \(x_2=1\); plug into equation 3.)
W2. Objective value. With the same \(A,b\) and trial \(x=(1,0.5)\), compute \(\|Ax-b\|\) (Euclidean). Is this the minimum? (You need not prove optimality yet — just evaluate the objective.)
W3. Closest attainable vector. Sketch (in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) as a cartoon, or think in words): \(C(A)\) is a plane (or line) through the origin; \(b\) is off the plane; \(\hat{b}=A\hat{x}\) is the foot of the perpendicular from \(b\) to \(C(A)\). Label the residual \(r=b-\hat{b}\).
W4. Exact case. Change \(b\) to \(b'=(1,2,3)\). Show that \(x=(1,1)\) solves \(Ax=b'\) exactly. What is the residual? What is \(\min_x\|Ax-b'\|\)?
W5. Language check. In one sentence each, distinguish “no solution” from “best approximate solution.”

title: Lecture 38 — When \(Ax=b\) has no exact solution
text:
Your turn
Y1. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad
b=\begin{bmatrix}3\\1\\1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
x=\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(Ax\) and \(r=b-Ax\). Is \(x\) an exact solution? What is \(\|r\|\)?
Y2. True or false, with a one-line reason: if \(Ax=b\) is inconsistent, then no vector \(\hat{x}\) can make \(\|A\hat{x}-b\|\) finite.
Y3. In words: what does \(\hat{b}=A\hat{x}\) represent when \(\hat{x}\) is a least-squares solution?
Y4. A \(4\times 2\) matrix \(A\) has linearly independent columns, and \(b\notin C(A)\). Can \(Ax=b\) have an exact solution? Can it have a least-squares solution?






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \(Ax=(2,1,1)\); \(r=(1,0,0)\); not exact. \(\|r\|=1\).
Y2. False. The residual norm is always finite; least squares still chooses an \(\hat{x}\) that minimizes it (even when the minimum is positive).
Y3. \(\hat{b}\) is the closest vector in the column space \(C(A)\) to the observed \(b\) — the attainable right-hand side under the model \(Ax\).
Y4. Exact: no (\(b\notin C(A)\)). Least squares: yes (minimizer of \(\|Ax-b\|\) still exists; uniqueness follows from independent columns).

title: Lecture 39 — Least squares, data fitting, and positive definiteness
text:
Warm-up
Monday’s setup: minimize \(\|Ax-b\|\). At a minimizer \(\hat{x}\), the residual \(r=b-A\hat{x}\) is orthogonal to \(C(A)\), which is equivalent to the normal equations \[
A^{\mathsf{T}}A\,\hat{x}=A^{\mathsf{T}}b.
\]

If \(A\) is \(m\times n\) with \(m>n\), what size is \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\)? Why is that nicer than solving \(Ax=b\) directly?
True or false: \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) is always symmetric.

title: Lecture 39 — Least squares, data fitting, and positive definiteness
text:
Fill in
Normal equations / software. Solving \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\hat{x}=A^{\mathsf{T}}b\) (when \(A\) has independent columns) gives the unique least-squares \(\hat{x}\). In practice we often call a solver instead of forming \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) by hand:








Task
Octave
Python




Least-squares \(\hat{x}\)
xhat = A \ b
xhat = np.linalg.lstsq(A, b, rcond=None)[0]


Fitted values
bhat = A*xhat
bhat = A @ xhat


Residual
r = b - bhat
r = b - bhat


RMS
rms = norm(r)/sqrt(m)
rms = np.linalg.norm(r)/np.sqrt(m)



Orthogonality check. At a least-squares solution, \(A^{\mathsf{T}}r \approx \underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\) (numerical noise ok).
RMS. Root-mean-square residual \(\mathrm{RMS}=\|r\|/\sqrt{m}\) reports a typical per-equation error in the same units as \(b\).
Useful vs coefficients. Always ask: do fitted values track the data? Is RMS small in context? Blindly quoting \(\hat{x}\) is not enough.
Positive semidefinite / definite (Boyd / class notes). A symmetric matrix \(P\) is positive semidefinite (PSD) if \(x^{\mathsf{T}}Px\ge 0\) for all \(x\); positive definite (PD) if \(x^{\mathsf{T}}Px>0\) for all \(x\neq 0\).
For any \(A\): \[
x^{\mathsf{T}}(A^{\mathsf{T}}A)x = \lVert Ax\rVert^2 \ge 0,
\] so \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) is always \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\). It is positive definite precisely when \(Ax=0\Rightarrow x=0\), i.e. when \(A\) has \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) columns — then the normal equations have a unique solution.

title: Lecture 40 — SVD, Lab 6, Quiz 11, and capstone launch
text:
Fill in
SVD (conceptual). Every real \(m\times n\) matrix factors as \[
A = U\Sigma V^{\mathsf{T}},
\] where the columns of \(U\) and \(V\) are orthonormal (left / right singular vectors) and \(\Sigma\) is rectangular “diagonal” with nonnegative singular values \[
\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge 0
\] on its main diagonal. Think: \(A\) = rotate/reflect → stretch by \(\sigma_i\) → rotate/reflect.
Rank-\(k\) approximation. Keep the largest \(k\) singular values (and matching singular-vector columns); set the rest to zero. The truncated product \[
A_k = U_k\Sigma_k V_k^{\mathsf{T}}
\] is the best rank-\(k\) approximation in the usual 2-norm / Frobenius sense (details in the slides / capstone).
Software sketch (capstone / later — not Lab 6 today):

Octave

Rank-\(k\) rebuild
use first \(k\) columns / \(\sigma\)’s
U[:,:k] @ np.diag(S[:k]) @ Vt[:k,:]

title: Capstone — Low-rank frames vs differences
text:
The question
You get (or build) three grayscale frames \(F_1,F_2,F_3\), each an \(m\times n\) matrix of intensities.
Compare two encoding strategies with rank-\(k\) SVD approximations:







Plan
What you compress with a rank-\(k\) SVD




A — Independent frames
\(F_1\), \(F_2\), and \(F_3\) separately


B — Frame + differences
\(F_1\), then \(D_2=F_2-F_1\), then \(D_3=F_3-F_2\)



Driving question: For your data, when (if ever) is Plan B better than Plan A on accuracy, storage, and runtime / resource use — including the cost of computing the SVDs?
Computing an SVD is not free. Low-rank storage or faster later multiplies only help when the matrix is well approximated at modest \(k\) and you reuse the representation enough (or care enough about storage/transmission) to justify the factorization cost. Image examples are instructional.

title: Capstone — Low-rank frames vs differences
text:
Technical notes
Storage (order of magnitude).

One full frame: \(mn\) numbers.
One rank-\(k\) factorization: about \(k(m+n+1)\) numbers (columns of \(U_k\), \(V_k\), and \(k\) singular values).
Plan A total (three frames): about \(3k(m+n+1)\).
Plan B total (three matrices): also about \(3k(m+n+1)\) at the same \(k\) — so Plan B wins on storage only if you can use a smaller \(k\) for differences while matching Plan A’s error, or if you choose different \(k\) per matrix on purpose.

Error. For a matrix \(A\) and approximation \(A_k\), a standard relative Frobenius error is \[
\frac{\lVert A-A_k\rVert_F}{\lVert A\rVert_F}.
\] Under Plan B, measure error on the reconstructed frames \(\widehat F_2=\widehat F_1+\widehat D_2\), etc., not only on the difference matrices.

title: Quiz 10
text:
Core

Fluency (complete prompts — practice these by hand)
C10.1. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{bmatrix}.
\] (a) Compute \(A^{-1}\) using the \(2\times 2\) formula (or by solving \(AB=I\)). (b) Check \(A^{-1}A=I\). (c) Solve \(Ax=(4,3)\) using \(x=A^{-1}b\).
C10.2. Decide whether each matrix is invertible. Give a one-line reason (dependent columns, \(Ax=0\), or \(\det\)).

\(\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix}\)
\(\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{bmatrix}\)
\(\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\)

C10.3. True or false, with a one-line reason: for a single right-hand side \(b\), forming \(A^{-1}\) explicitly and then computing \(A^{-1}b\) is generally preferable to solving \(Ax=b\) with a solver / elimination.
C10.4. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & 0 \\
2 & 4 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}.
\] The RREF of \(A\) is \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1 \\
0 & 0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\] (after row swaps / scaling as needed — use this RREF). Find \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\), a basis for \(C(A)\) using original columns, and a basis for \(N(A)\).
C10.5. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 \\
2 & 0 \\
0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}.
\] Describe \(C(A)\) in words. Is \(b=(1,2,3)\) in \(C(A)\)? Find a basis for \(N(A)\) (or state that \(N(A)=\{0\}\)).
C10.6. True or false, with a one-line reason: if \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=n\) for an \(m\times n\) matrix with \(m\ge n\), then \(Ax=0\) has only the zero solution.
C10.7. Compute each determinant.

\(\det\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix}\)
\(\det\begin{bmatrix}1&4&0\\0&-2&5\\0&0&3\end{bmatrix}\)
\(\det\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\4&2\end{bmatrix}\)

C10.8. Let \(A=\begin{bmatrix}0&-2\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\). Compute \(\det A\). Where do \(e_1\) and \(e_2\) go under \(x\mapsto Ax\)? What area does the unit square map to?
C10.9. True or false, with a one-line reason: if \(\det A=0\) for square \(A\), then \(A\) is not invertible and \(Ax=b\) fails to have a unique solution for every \(b\).
C10.10. Connect the ideas. For square \(A\), match each statement to the equivalent view (write the letter):


\(A\) is invertible


\(\operatorname{rank}(A)=n\) (full)


\(\det A\neq 0\)


\(N(A)=\{0\}\)


Which of (ii)–(iv) are equivalent to (i)?
C10.11 (cumulative, light). Let \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{bmatrix}\). What geometric map is \(x\mapsto Ax\)? Is \(A\) invertible? What is \(\det A\)?

title: Quiz 11
text:
Core

Fluency (complete prompts � practice these by hand)
C11.1. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix},\qquad
v=\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(Av\). Is \(v\) an eigenvector? If so, what is \(\lambda\)?
C11.2. You are told that \(v=(2,-1)\) is an eigenvector of \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}4&2\\1&3\end{bmatrix}.
\] Find \(\lambda\) by comparing components of \(Av\) and \(v\). Then verify \(Av=\lambda v\).
C11.3. Let \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1.2,\,0.5)\) (Lab 4 / Lecture 35 long-run pattern).

Name two real eigenpairs using the standard basis.
If \(x_0=(1,1)\), write \(x_t=A^t x_0\) componentwise. Which term dominates for large \(t\)?

C11.4. Complex drill. Let \(z=2+i\) and \(w=1-3i\). Compute \(z+w\), \(zw\), and \(|z|\).
C11.5. For \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&3\end{bmatrix},
\] form \(\det(A-\lambda I)\), find both eigenvalues, and give one eigenvector for \(\lambda=3\).
C11.6. Rotation. Let \(R=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\) (\(90^\circ\) CCW).

Show that the characteristic polynomial is \(\lambda^2+1=0\), so \(\lambda=\pm i\).
Why does this match the geometric fact that \(R\) has no real eigenvector?

C11.7. Check a complex pair. With \(A=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\) and \(v=(1,-i)\), compute \(Av\) and decide whether \(Av=iv\) or \(Av=(-i)v\).
C11.8. True or false, with a one-line reason: if \(Av=2v\) and \(v\neq 0\), then \(A^3 v=8v\).
C11.9 (Lab 5 / software). Suppose Octave/Python reports eigenvalues of a \(2\times 2\) matrix as approximately \(0.9\) and \(0.2\), with corresponding eigenvectors \(v_1\approx(0.7,\,0.7)\) and \(v_2\approx(-0.7,\,0.7)\) (normalized). For dynamics \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\) started near \(v_1+v_2\), which mode dominates for large \(t\), and does the state grow or decay?
C11.10 (Lab 5 / verify). Software prints \(\lambda\approx 3\) and \(v\approx(0.707,\,0.707)\) for \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}.
\] Explain how you would verify \(Av\approx\lambda v\) numerically in one or two lines of code (Octave or Python). What should \(\|Av-\lambda v\|\) look like if the pair is correct?

title: Course Syllabus
text:
Course Description (Catalog Description)
Euclidean spaces, matrices and matrix arithmetic, solving systems of equations, and eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Emphasis on applications and use of computation.
Division: Lower Division.
Weekly: Lecture 3 hrs.
Instruction Mode: Face to face only.
Prerequisite: (MATH 101 and MATH 101T) or MATH 102 or ALEKS PPL assessment score 78–100 or appropriate high school coursework. All prerequisite courses must be passed with a grade of C− or higher. See Math Placement and ALEKS PPL for details.
Note: if you plan to use MATH 107 as a prerequisite for another MATH, DATA, or STAT course, you must have a grade of C− or better in this course.

Course Learning Outcomes
By the end of this course, students will be able to:

Interpret matrices, vectors, and complex numbers, both algebraically and geometrically.
Solve systems of linear equations using row-reduction techniques by hand and with software.
Find eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix by hand for a \(2\times 2\) matrix and with software for general cases.
Understand and apply eigenvalues and eigenvectors to solve problems.
Recognize special types of matrices and their properties, such as triangular, symmetric, and positive definite matrices.
Communicate in the language of linear algebra, including linear combination, subspace, span, independence, basis, and dimension.
Write or adapt programs to implement linear algebra concepts, such as matrix arithmetic, vectors, and plotting.
Apply linear algebra to real-world problems.
Learn independently as well as collaboratively. Develop study techniques that include pre- and post-reading of class materials and be able to critically analyze and implement solutions in a team setting.

Daily learning objectives for each meeting are on Lectures.


General Education & Institutional Learning Outcomes
This course fulfills Lower Division General Education Area 2 (Mathematics) and supports Cal Poly Humboldt’s Institutional Learning Outcomes related to quantitative reasoning, critical thinking, and communication.

Late or Missed Work Policies
The policies for late or missed work are as follows:

Lecture attendance is required, but I know that sometimes you will need to miss class due to illness or other emergencies. Each student may miss up to 10 lecture days without penalty and without contacting me. Reserve these days for emergencies. In my experience, it is rare for a student to succeed if they regularly miss class or are absent for more than two weeks, so if you find yourself in that situation, please communicate with me and your advisor so we can help you find a solution.
Quizzes are in the first 10 minutes of class. The lowest two quiz scores are dropped. If you must miss a quiz due to illness or another emergency, please contact me to arrange a makeup.
Labs are credited in class on the dates on the schedule: complete the hub exercises, handwrite the one-pager, and get initials. After a week, missed lab credit is not made up except by arrangement (e.g. illness).
Capstone work is due on the dates on the schedule. Late project work cannot be turned in due to the end of the semester and course grades being due. If you are unable to complete the project in time, you should consider whether your situation is such that an Incomplete grade is appropriate. This would give you more time to complete the course.
Midterms and the final exam are required. If you need to miss a midterm due to illness or another emergency, communicate with me as soon as possible to reschedule.

Note: Technology issues (internet access, device failure, software problems) are not automatically considered valid excuses for late or missed work; students are expected to plan accordingly.


AI Policy
Much of your course grade will be based on work you produce in class (quizzes and exams) without having the option of using AI as a resource.
Outside of in-class assessments, you may use AI, such as NotebookLM or ChatGPT, to help you learn the material or to get unstuck on labs or the capstone.
For work that you do at home that is turned in for a grade I have two requirements:

If you used AI, acknowledge this briefly in the document (you don’t need to state in detail how you used AI or give your prompts, just the name of the AI service you used).
Be responsible for the correctness and appropriateness of all (AI-assisted or not) materials you turn in.

I may use AI to assist me in my delivery of the course material, such as asking whether an assignment is appropriate for a college-level course or whether the wording of a quiz question could be improved. I will not use AI to grade your work or use an AI detection tool to check your work.
